claim: Spontaneously varying pupil size correlates with power of brain activity in most frequency bands across large-scale resting state cortical networks.
source: Spontaneously varying pupil size correlates with power of brain activity in most frequency bands across large-scale resting state cortical networks.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from simultaneous MEG and pupil recordings showing correlations between pupil size and spectral power across multiple frequency bands and networks, as shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Pupil size recorded at prestimulus baseline correlates with subsequent shifts in detection bias (c).
source: Pupil size recorded at prestimulus baseline correlates with subsequent shifts in detection bias (c) and sensitivity (d').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the perceptual decision-making task showing that prestimulus pupil size predicts changes in detection criterion, as shown in Figure 4C and Table 1.

claim: Pupil size recorded at prestimulus baseline correlates with subsequent shifts in sensitivity (d').
source: Pupil size recorded at prestimulus baseline correlates with subsequent shifts in detection bias (c) and sensitivity (d').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing an inverted U-shaped relationship between prestimulus pupil size and detection sensitivity, as shown in Figure 4C and Table 1.

claim: When dissociated from pupil-linked state, prestimulus spectral power of resting state networks still predicts perceptual behavior.
source: When dissociated from pupil-linked state, prestimulus spectral power of resting state networks still predicts perceptual behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that residual spectral power (independent of pupil size) predicts behavioral outcomes, as shown in Figure 5.

claim: Fast spontaneous pupil constriction and dilation correlate with large-scale brain activity.
source: Fast spontaneous pupil constriction and dilation correlate with large-scale brain activity as well but not perceptual behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing cross-correlation between pupil events and MEG activity, as shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: Fast spontaneous pupil constriction and dilation do not correlate with perceptual behavior.
source: Fast spontaneous pupil constriction and dilation correlate with large-scale brain activity as well but not perceptual behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no difference in behavioral metrics when stimuli were presented during constriction versus dilation events, as shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Larger pupil or more desynchronized (i.e., higher-frequency) brain activity generally correspond to higher arousal.
source: Larger pupil or more desynchronized (i.e., higher-frequency) brain activity generally correspond to higher arousal.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about arousal markers in neuroscience.

claim: The two arousal markers (pupil size and spectral content of cortical activity) correlate with each other in animals.
source: While the two arousal markers correlate with each other in animals (Stitt et al., 2018; McGinley et al., 2015b; Joshi et al., 2016; Yüzgeç et al., 2018; McGinley et al., 2015a; Reimer et al., 2014), they historically have motivated two separate lines of research in humans (outlined below).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous animal studies.

claim: The Yerkes–Dodson law (1908) describes behavioral performance in difficult tasks as an inverted-U function of arousal.
source: The Yerkes–Dodson law (1908) (Yerkes and Dodson, 1908) describes behavioral performance in difficult tasks as an inverted-U function of arousal, where intermediate levels of arousal (inferred from pupil size) are most beneficial to task performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the original Yerkes and Dodson work.

claim: Intermediate levels of arousal (inferred from pupil size) are most beneficial to task performance according to the Yerkes-Dodson law.
source: The Yerkes–Dodson law (1908) (Yerkes and Dodson, 1908) describes behavioral performance in difficult tasks as an inverted-U function of arousal, where intermediate levels of arousal (inferred from pupil size) are most beneficial to task performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the Yerkes-Dodson law.

claim: The Yerkes-Dodson law has been criticized for not taking into account that performance efficiency cannot be captured by a single behavioral variable in most tasks.
source: This law has been criticized, however, for not taking into account that performance efficiency cannot be captured by a single behavioral variable in most tasks (Eysenck, 1982) and later studies have focused on more extensive research of pupil-linked behavior (e.g., Kahneman and Beatty, 1966).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Eysenck, 1982.

claim: Baseline pupil size predicts perceptual decisions in humans.
source: A few recent studies show that baseline pupil size predicts perceptual decisions in humans (Waschke et al., 2019; van Kempen et al., 2019) and animals (McGinley et al., 2015a; Steinmetz et al., 2019), but the timescale of the arousal fluctuations shaping behavior and their underlying cortical mechanisms remain poorly understood.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent human studies.

claim: Baseline pupil size predicts perceptual decisions in animals.
source: A few recent studies show that baseline pupil size predicts perceptual decisions in humans (Waschke et al., 2019; van Kempen et al., 2019) and animals (McGinley et al., 2015a; Steinmetz et al., 2019), but the timescale of the arousal fluctuations shaping behavior and their underlying cortical mechanisms remain poorly understood.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: Changes in cortical spectral power within the waking state predict trial-to-trial variations in behavior.
source: More recent research reveals that changes in cortical spectral power within the waking state (e.g., measured as prestimulus baseline spectral power) also predict (trial-to-trial) variations in behavior.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the research literature discussed in the introduction.

claim: Broadband changes in cortical spectral power correlate with moment-to-moment arousal fluctuation and influence behavioral performance in animals.
source: At this timescale, while some animal studies show that broadband changes in cortical spectral power correlate with moment-to-moment arousal fluctuation and influence behavioral performance (McGinley et al., 2015b; Sederberg et al., 2019), human studies mostly focus on band-limited power with no control for spontaneous arousal shifts (Linkenkaer-Hansen et al., 2004; Wyart and Tallon-Baudry, 2009; Arnal et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: Human studies on spectral power and behavior mostly focus on band-limited power with no control for spontaneous arousal shifts.
source: At this timescale, while some animal studies show that broadband changes in cortical spectral power correlate with moment-to-moment arousal fluctuation and influence behavioral performance (McGinley et al., 2015b; Sederberg et al., 2019), human studies mostly focus on band-limited power with no control for spontaneous arousal shifts (Linkenkaer-Hansen et al., 2004; Wyart and Tallon-Baudry, 2009; Arnal et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human studies.

claim: Prestimulus power in the alpha band inversely relates to stimulus detection.
source: For example, prestimulus power in the alpha band (Samaha et al., 2020) inversely relates to stimulus detection (Ergenoglu et al., 2004; van Dijk et al., 2008; Limbach and Corballis, 2016; Busch et al., 2009) and attentional allocation (Jensen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Prestimulus alpha power relates to attentional allocation.
source: For example, prestimulus power in the alpha band (Samaha et al., 2020) inversely relates to stimulus detection (Ergenoglu et al., 2004; van Dijk et al., 2008; Limbach and Corballis, 2016; Busch et al., 2009) and attentional allocation (Jensen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jensen et al., 2012.

claim: Pupil-linked arousal and desynchronization in auditory cortex have distinct contributions to perceptual behavior.
source: Supporting this distinction, a recent study (Waschke et al., 2019) showed that pupil-linked arousal and desynchronization in auditory cortex have distinct contributions to perceptual behavior, but this study only investigated the auditory cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Waschke et al., 2019.

claim: MEG provides superior signal-to-noise ratio for investigating brain activity.
source: MEG provides superior signal-to-noise ratio and source modeling allowed us to investigate the unique behavioral contributions of spectral power modulation in different large-scale brain networks.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about MEG as a neuroimaging technique.

claim: Pupil size fluctuations reflect antagonistic shifts in spectral power between low-frequency and high-frequency bands.
source: We show that pupil size fluctuations reflect antagonistic shifts in spectral power between low-frequency and high-frequency bands, while the intermediate alpha band relates to pupil size according to an inverted-U function.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing opposite relationships between pupil size and low vs. high frequency power, as shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The intermediate alpha band relates to pupil size according to an inverted-U function.
source: We show that pupil size fluctuations reflect antagonistic shifts in spectral power between low-frequency and high-frequency bands, while the intermediate alpha band relates to pupil size according to an inverted-U function.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing a quadratic relationship between alpha power and pupil size, as shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both pupil-linked and pupil-independent brain states influence perceptual decision-making, albeit in different manners.
source: Both pupil-linked and pupil-independent brain states influence perceptual decision-making, albeit in different manners.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing distinct behavioral effects of pupil-linked arousal and residual spectral power, as shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The prestimulus brain state influencing perceptual decisions contains a strong component linked to global electrophysiological arousal fluctuations in conjunction with the unique contributions of specific frequency bands localized to specialized brain networks.
source: These findings indicate that the prestimulus brain state influencing perceptual decisions contains a strong component linked to global electrophysiological arousal fluctuations in conjunction with the unique contributions of specific frequency bands localized to specialized brain networks.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined results showing both global arousal effects and network-specific spectral power effects on behavior.

claim: 24 participants were included in the study.
source: We simultaneously monitored pupil size and brain activity (using MEG) in 24 participants during eyes-open rest and a visual perceptual decision-making task (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study design.

claim: Two 5 min rest sessions were acquired in 21 participants and one rest session in the three remaining participants.
source: We acquired two 5 min rest sessions in 21 participants and one rest session in the three remaining participants (see Materials and methods and Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: The task included long prestimulus intervals (3–6 s) wherein a fixation cross on a gray background was identical to the one used in eyes-open rest sessions.
source: The task included long prestimulus intervals (3–6 s) wherein a fixation cross on a gray background was identical to the one used in eyes-open rest sessions (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: The power spectrum of pupil size fluctuations is dominated by power in low frequencies, exhibiting a 1/f-type spectrum.
source: The power spectrum of pupil size fluctuations is dominated by power in low frequencies, exhibiting a 1/f-type spectrum, consistent with previous reports (Yellin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and citation to previous work.

claim: Rapid and longer-lasting pupil dilations are associated with phasic activity of LC noradrenergic (LC-NE) projections and sustained activity in basal forebrain cholinergic (BF-Ach) projections, respectively.
source: Animal studies show that fast pupil events are regulated by neural activity in cortex, superior colliculi, and locus coeruleus (LC) (Joshi et al., 2016; Reimer et al., 2014; Reimer et al., 2016), with distinct neuromodulatory control as compared to slow pupil states: rapid and longer-lasting pupil dilations are associated with phasic activity of LC noradrenergic (LC-NE) projections and sustained activity in basal forebrain cholinergic (BF-Ach) projections, respectively (Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to animal studies.

claim: High-frequency (beta-gamma) power increases with larger pupil size.
source: These results show widely distributed changes in power with slow fluctuations of pupil size: low-frequency (delta) power decreases and high-frequency (beta-gamma) power increases with larger pupil size.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Widespread cortical activity modulation by pupil size could stem from the activity of neuromodulatory systems that regulate pupil size, such as the LC system, with LC-NE axons projecting widely to many cortical areas.
source: Such widespread cortical activity modulation could stem from the activity of neuromodulatory systems that regulate pupil size, such as the LC system, with LC-NE axons projecting widely to many cortical areas (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data combined with citation to previous work on neuromodulatory systems.

claim: Human and monkey functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies report correlations between pupil size and activity in large-scale resting state networks (RSNs).
source: Because human (Yellin et al., 2015) and monkey (Chang et al., 2016) functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies report correlations between pupil size and activity in large-scale resting state networks (RSNs), we used a functional atlas (Yeo et al., 2011) estimated from a large resting state fMRI dataset (N = 1000) by clustering functionally connected cortical areas into seven large-scale RSNs (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to fMRI studies.

claim: The inverted U-shaped relationship between alpha power and pupil size is consistent with a previous EEG study.
source: This finding is consistent with a previous EEG study (Hong et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hong et al., 2014.

claim: Eyes-open alpha power does not index transitioning to a state of relaxation ('idling') as was traditionally considered in EEG research.
source: Consistent with recent suggestions (Sadaghiani and Kleinschmidt, 2016; Clayton et al., 2018), these results indicate that eyes-open alpha power does not index transitioning to a state of relaxation ('idling') as was traditionally considered in EEG research.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data combined with citations to recent suggestions.

claim: A positive correlation between beta power and pupil size was recently observed in EEG, but not in the gamma range.
source: Such a positive correlation was recently observed in the EEG beta range, but not in the gamma range (Waschke et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Waschke et al., 2019.

claim: The inconsistency in the gamma range between the current study and previous EEG work may stem from the superior MEG sensitivity to high-frequency activity.
source: The inconsistency in the gamma range may stem from the superior MEG sensitivity to high-frequency activity.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about methodological differences.

claim: The image contrast was titrated for each participant in a pre-task staircase procedure, such that the same image was reported as recognized in 44.9% ± 3.5% of trials during the main task.
source: Briefly, the task entails recognition and categorization of liminal object images (Figure 1C): the image contrast was titrated for each participant in a pre-task staircase procedure, such that the same image was reported as recognized in 44.9% ± 3.5% (i.e., %'yes' reports, mean ± s.e.m., N = 24) of trials during the main task, not significantly different from the intended 50% recognition rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the task.

claim: Hit rate increases with baseline pupil size.
source: Our results indicate that hit rate (i.e., proportion of 'yes' responses to images containing real objects) increases with baseline pupil size (Figure 4C), whereby both model types produce significant positive linear component (p < 0.05, see Table 1 for exact statistics).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Table 1.

claim: False alarm rate did not change with pupil size.
source: By contrast, false alarm rate did not change with pupil size.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Table 1.

claim: Detection criterion linearly decreases (i.e., becoming more liberal) with increasing pupil size.
source: We observed that detection criterion linearly decreases (i.e., becoming more liberal) with increasing pupil size (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Table 1.

claim: Sensitivity (d') is related with prestimulus pupil size in an inverted U-shaped relationship, potentially following the classic Yerkes–Dodson law.
source: Sensitivity (d') is related with prestimulus pupil size in an inverted U-shaped relationship, potentially following the classic Yerkes–Dodson law (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Table 1, with speculation about connection to Yerkes-Dodson law.

claim: Faster and more accurate object categorization responses follow larger baseline pupil size.
source: We also observed faster and more accurate object categorization responses following larger baseline pupil size (Figure 4D, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Table 1.

claim: Pupil-linked states significantly affected the stimulus-triggered category representation.
source: Importantly, pupil-linked states significantly affected the stimulus-triggered category representation (F = 2.97, p = 0.03), with larger pupil size preceding better neural representation of stimulus category, consistently with a previous report (Warren et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from decoding analysis shown in Figure 4E and citation to Warren et al., 2016.

claim: All logistic regression models predict 'yes'/'no' behavior better than chance.
source: We find that all logistic regression models predict 'yes'/'no' behavior better than chance (permutation test, p < 0.05 FDR-corrected).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The performance of 'power only' model does not improve by adding pupil size information.
source: Interestingly, the performance of 'power only' model does not improve by adding pupil size information (W = 143, p = 0.86, Wilcoxon signed-rank test), but the performance is worsened by regressing out the pupil-linked spectral power (W = 241, p = 0.008, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical tests shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Both arousal-linked and arousal-independent spectral power fluctuations at baseline predict subsequent recognition behavior.
source: These results indicate that both arousal-linked and arousal-independent spectral power fluctuations at baseline predict subsequent recognition behavior, but our recordings of pupil size did not provide additional information contributing to the prediction of behavior that was not already present in cortical spectral power.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the logistic regression model results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Pupil-independent negative correlation of power in delta and theta bands with hit rate was observed, with the largest effect size in the visual RSN.
source: Analysis using the linear model (Equation 5) revealed pupil-independent negative correlation of power in delta and theta bands with hit rate, with the largest effect size in the visual RSN (Figure 5B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Alpha and beta power in visual RSN negatively correlated with hit rate.
source: Alpha and beta power in visual RSN also negatively correlated with hit rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Residual delta power in the dorsal attention network (DAN) and visual network has an effect on detection criterion, such that higher delta power results in a more conservative criterion.
source: Using SDT analysis, we found that residual delta power in the dorsal attention network (DAN) and visual network has an effect on detection criterion, such that higher delta power results in a more conservative criterion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: DAN includes the decision-making-related frontal eye field (FEF) and posterior parietal cortex areas.
source: DAN includes the decision-making-related frontal eye field (FEF) and posterior parietal cortex areas (Dorris and Glimcher, 2004), which were shown to reflect decision criterion in non-human primates (Gold and Shadlen, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Detection sensitivity, but not criterion, was influenced by pupil-independent alpha power in the visual and default mode RSNs.
source: Interestingly, detection sensitivity, but not criterion, was influenced by pupil-independent alpha power in the visual and default mode RSNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Brain activity recorded from most MEG sensors correlated with pupil diameter at a fast timescale.
source: Brain activity recorded from most MEG sensors correlated with pupil diameter at this fast timescale (Figure 6A; spatiotemporal cluster-based permutation test, p < 0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The correlation values between MEG activity and pupil size were highest at a lag of 400 ms in most MEG sensors.
source: The correlation values were highest at a lag of 400 ms in most MEG sensors (Figure 6B), suggesting that cortical activity precedes fast pupil events by ~400 ms.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Cortical activity precedes fast pupil events by ~400 ms.
source: The correlation values were highest at a lag of 400 ms in most MEG sensors (Figure 6B), suggesting that cortical activity precedes fast pupil events by ~400 ms.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Both dilation- and constriction-related MEG activity shows one peak and one trough at ~0 and –400 ms.
source: Both dilation- and constriction-related MEG activity shows one peak and one trough at ~0 and –400 ms.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Whether a liminal visual stimulus is presented during ongoing pupil dilation or constriction did not influence perceptual behavior in the task.
source: Such a potential influence, however, does not seem to be behaviorally relevant: whether a liminal visual stimulus is presented during ongoing pupil dilation or constriction did not influence perceptual behavior in our task (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Pupil-linked arousal covaries with spontaneous widespread changes in electrophysiological brain activity in humans.
source: Our data suggest that pupil-linked arousal covaries with spontaneous widespread changes in electrophysiological brain activity in humans (Figures 2 and 3, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–4, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: This widespread arousal effect on cortical activity is consistent with previous human fMRI studies showing that large-scale fluctuations of BOLD signal in the resting state correlate with pupil size.
source: This widespread arousal effect on cortical activity is consistent with previous human fMRI studies showing that large-scale fluctuations of BOLD signal in the resting state correlate with pupil size (Yellin et al., 2015; Shine et al., 2016; Schneider et al., 2016), as well as the widespread cortical projections from subcortical neuromodulatory systems including the LC-NE or BF-ACh systems.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to fMRI studies and knowledge about neuromodulatory systems.

claim: Activity of both LC-NE and BF-ACh systems correlates with pupil size and cortical activity in mice and non-human primates.
source: Activity of both systems correlates with pupil size and cortical activity in mice (Reimer et al., 2016) and non-human primates (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005, Turchi et al., 2018), but only limited data is available in humans (de Gee et al., 2017, Murphy et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: The 1/f exponent decreases during high arousal states, leading to simultaneous increase of high-frequency power and decrease of low-frequency power.
source: Because the effect of pupil-linked arousal spans all frequencies, it likely stems at least partly from aperiodic brain activity, where the 1/f exponent decreases during high arousal sates, leading to simultaneous increase of high-frequency power and decrease of low-frequency power.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data and knowledge about 1/f spectral properties.

claim: The 1/f exponent of intracranial EEG power spectrum in the frequency range of 30–45 Hz is smaller (i.e., the power spectrum is shallower) in wakefulness than under anesthesia.
source: Indeed, a recent study demonstrated that 1/f exponent of intracranial EEG power spectrum in the frequency range of 30–45 Hz is smaller (i.e., the power spectrum is shallower) in wakefulness than under anesthesia, pointing to the effect in the expected direction (Lendner et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lendner et al., 2020.

claim: BF-ACh activity and increase in pupil size are associated with spectral modulation following the same principle: increase in high-frequency and decrease in low-frequency power.
source: Furthermore, both BF-ACh (Szerb, 1967) and LC-NE (Berridge and Waterhouse, 2003) activity and increase in pupil size (McGinley et al., 2015a; Reimer et al., 2014; Vinck et al., 2015; Stitt et al., 2018) are associated with spectral modulation following the same principle: increase in high-frequency and decrease in low-frequency power.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: An inverted U-shaped relationship between alpha power and pupil size was observed in the resting state and prestimulus baseline, consistent with recent EEG studies.
source: We observed an inverted U-shaped relationship between alpha power and pupil size in the resting state and prestimulus baseline, consistent with recent EEG studies (van Kempen et al., 2019; Hong et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to EEG studies.

claim: Alpha power positively correlates with tonic alertness.
source: This relationship between prestimulus alpha power and pupil size is consistent with a previous suggestion that alpha power positively correlates with tonic alertness (Sadaghiani and Kleinschmidt, 2016; Sadaghiani et al., 2010), which might correspond to the dominant left-hand side of the inverted-U function (Figure 3B); further, the inverted U-shaped relationship we observed is consistent with the disappearance of alpha oscillations during drowsiness and light sleep—states with very low arousal (Cantero et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Alpha oscillations disappear during drowsiness and light sleep—states with very low arousal.
source: This relationship between prestimulus alpha power and pupil size is consistent with a previous suggestion that alpha power positively correlates with tonic alertness (Sadaghiani and Kleinschmidt, 2016; Sadaghiani et al., 2010), which might correspond to the dominant left-hand side of the inverted-U function (Figure 3B); further, the inverted U-shaped relationship we observed is consistent with the disappearance of alpha oscillations during drowsiness and light sleep—states with very low arousal (Cantero et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cantero et al., 1999.

claim: Modulation of alpha power by arousal in the visual RSN is stronger than in other networks at rest.
source: We observed, for example, differences in parameter estimates across networks and behavioral conditions: modulation of alpha power by arousal in the visual RSN is stronger than in other networks at rest, whereas modulation of beta power is strongest in the DAN in task baseline (Figure 3C, linear components).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Modulation of beta power is strongest in the DAN in task baseline.
source: We observed, for example, differences in parameter estimates across networks and behavioral conditions: modulation of alpha power by arousal in the visual RSN is stronger than in other networks at rest, whereas modulation of beta power is strongest in the DAN in task baseline (Figure 3C, linear components).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Pupil-linked arousal systems may play an important role in dynamic reconfiguration of large-scale networks topology responding to cognitive demands.
source: Such non-uniform effects are consistent with the intriguing proposals of pupil-linked arousal systems playing an important role in dynamic reconfiguration of large-scale networks topology responding to cognitive demands (van den Brink et al., 2019; Shine, 2019).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data combined with citations to theoretical proposals.

claim: Recent studies report complex topographic organization of neuromodulatory systems which may produce non-uniform modulatory effects.
source: Indeed, while the arousal neuromodulatory systems send widespread projections to cortex, recent studies also report complex topographic organization which may produce such non-uniform modulatory effects (Uematsu et al., 2017; Chandler et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: An inverted U-shaped relationship between perceptual sensitivity and prestimulus pupil size was observed in a previous auditory discrimination study.
source: A previous study (Waschke et al., 2019) using an auditory discrimination task observed a similar inverted-U function between perceptual sensitivity and prestimulus pupil size as we observed here.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Waschke et al., 2019.

claim: A null effect of baseline pupil size on behavior was reported in a previous visual detection study.
source: A null effect of baseline pupil size on behavior was reported in a previous visual detection study (de Gee et al., 2017), but the analyzed baseline period in this study coincided with the appearance of a noise stimulus, which may have influenced pupil diameter during the baseline period.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to de Gee et al., 2017 with speculation about methodological differences.

claim: An inverted U-shaped relationship between baseline pupil size and subsequent hit rate and detection sensitivity was reported in the mouse.
source: An inverted U-shaped relationship between baseline pupil size and subsequent hit rate and detection sensitivity was reported in the mouse (McGinley et al., 2015a; Steinmetz et al., 2019), consistent with our findings.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to mouse studies.

claim: Criterion was reported to follow a U-shaped function with baseline pupil size in mice.
source: Criterion was reported to follow a U-shaped function with baseline pupil size (McGinley et al., 2015a); our data is consistent with the left-hand side of this relationship, potentially due to the mouse achieving higher arousal levels during the experiment.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to McGinley et al., 2015a with speculation about differences in arousal range.

claim: The adaptive gain theory postulates that ongoing changes in pupil size reflect transitions between several states: exploration, when the tonic LC activity is high and the pupil is large; exploitation, when the LC activity is bursty and the pupil is of intermediate size; and drowsiness, when the tonic LC activity is low and the pupil is small.
source: Extending the classic Yerkes–Dodson law, the adaptive gain theory (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005) postulates that ongoing changes in pupil size reflect transitions between several states: exploration, when the tonic LC activity is high and the pupil is large; exploitation, when the LC activity is bursty and the pupil is of intermediate size; and drowsiness, when the tonic LC activity is low and the pupil is small.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the adaptive gain theory.

claim: The lowest perceptual sensitivity was observed with the smallest pupil size, which might be explained by low arousal or drowsiness.
source: Here, we observed the lowest perceptual sensitivity with the smallest pupil size (Figure 4C), which might be explained by low arousal or drowsiness.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The largest prestimulus pupil cooccurs with a subsequent shift to a more liberal decision criterion, which intuitively fits with the adaptive gain theory framework because exploration requires accepting a less rewarding option.
source: Interestingly, the largest prestimulus pupil also cooccurs with a subsequent shift to a more liberal decision criterion, which intuitively fits with the adaptive gain theory framework because exploration requires accepting a less rewarding option.
evidence: This claim is based on inference connecting the data to the adaptive gain theory framework.

claim: A larger baseline pupil diameter precedes more exploratory choices.
source: It has been shown indeed that a larger baseline pupil diameter precedes more exploratory choices (Jepma and Nieuwenhuis, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jepma and Nieuwenhuis, 2011.

claim: Recognition behavior ('yes'/'no' reports) could be predicted better than chance from single-trial baseline spectral power.
source: Interestingly, recognition behavior ('yes'/'no' reports) could be predicted better than chance from single-trial baseline spectral power and, while pupil size did not provide additional predictive power to the model, removing the pupil-linked spectral power fluctuations significantly reduced the model performance (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Behavior in a visual perceptual decision-making task is influenced by both arousal-linked and arousal-independent fluctuations of cortical spectral power.
source: This result indicates that behavior in a visual perceptual decision-making task is influenced by both arousal-linked and arousal-independent fluctuations of cortical spectral power.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the logistic regression model results.

claim: Prestimulus alpha power is modulated by both pupil-linked and pupil-independent mechanisms.
source: Our results indicate that, first, prestimulus alpha power is modulated by both pupil-linked and pupil-independent mechanisms; and second, the pupil-independent alpha power fluctuation appears to affect perceptual sensitivity but not criterion, while pupil-linked arousal influences both sensitivity and criterion.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined results of pupil-linked and residual power analyses.

claim: The pupil-independent alpha power fluctuation appears to affect perceptual sensitivity but not criterion, while pupil-linked arousal influences both sensitivity and criterion.
source: Our results indicate that, first, prestimulus alpha power is modulated by both pupil-linked and pupil-independent mechanisms; and second, the pupil-independent alpha power fluctuation appears to affect perceptual sensitivity but not criterion, while pupil-linked arousal influences both sensitivity and criterion.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined results shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Alpha power modulation plays an important role in attentional gating, such that alpha power suppression corresponds to the allocation of spatial- and feature-based attention.
source: Previous studies have also shown that alpha power modulation plays an important role in attentional gating, such that alpha power suppression corresponds to the allocation of spatial- and feature-based attention (Foxe and Snyder, 2011; Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Attentional cueing typically increases detection accuracy and sensitivity (d').
source: Given that attentional cueing typically increases detection accuracy (Haegens et al., 2011; Voytek and Knight, 2010) and sensitivity (d') (Kelly et al., 2009; Smith, 2000), our observed negative relationship between pupil-independent alpha power and detection sensitivity is consistent with the attention effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Spontaneous fMRI activity in DAN was shown to correlate with subsequent stimulus detection in humans.
source: Consistent with our result, spontaneous fMRI activity in DAN was shown to correlate with subsequent stimulus detection in humans (Boly et al., 2007; Sadaghiani et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to fMRI studies.

claim: Previous fMRI research revealed an effect of prestimulus DAN activity on subjective perceptual bias in a random dot motion detection task.
source: Previous fMRI research also revealed an effect of prestimulus DAN activity on subjective perceptual bias in a random dot motion detection task (Rahnev et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rahnev et al., 2012.

claim: FEF and posterior parietal cortex were shown to reflect decision criterion in non-human primates.
source: DAN includes the decision-making-related FEF and posterior parietal cortex (Dorris and Glimcher, 2004), which were shown to reflect decision criterion in non-human primates (Gold and Shadlen, 2007); electrical stimulation of FEF also affects the pupil size, potentially due to mechanisms related to selective attention (Ebitz et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gold and Shadlen, 2007.

claim: Electrical stimulation of FEF affects the pupil size, potentially due to mechanisms related to selective attention.
source: DAN includes the decision-making-related FEF and posterior parietal cortex (Dorris and Glimcher, 2004), which were shown to reflect decision criterion in non-human primates (Gold and Shadlen, 2007); electrical stimulation of FEF also affects the pupil size, potentially due to mechanisms related to selective attention (Ebitz et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ebitz et al., 2017.

claim: Spontaneous variations in MEG activity precede spontaneous variations in the pupil size with a lag of 400 ms.
source: Pupil size correlates with large-scale MEG activity on a faster timescale as well: first, spontaneous variations in MEG activity precede spontaneous variations in the pupil size with a lag of 400 ms (Figure 6A–B); second, pupillary events (constriction and dilation) coincide with MEG activity peak at lag zero and are preceded by an MEG activity peak occurring 400 ms earlier (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Pupillary events (constriction and dilation) coincide with MEG activity peak at lag zero and are preceded by an MEG activity peak occurring 400 ms earlier.
source: Pupil size correlates with large-scale MEG activity on a faster timescale as well: first, spontaneous variations in MEG activity precede spontaneous variations in the pupil size with a lag of 400 ms (Figure 6A–B); second, pupillary events (constriction and dilation) coincide with MEG activity peak at lag zero and are preceded by an MEG activity peak occurring 400 ms earlier (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: A similar pattern of two peaks (at 0 and –300 ms) was observed in monkey LC spike rates.
source: A similar pattern of two peaks (at 0 and –300 ms) was observed in monkey LC spike rates (Joshi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Joshi et al., 2016.

claim: The peak at –400 ms lag could point to an influence of cortical resting state fluctuations on LC activity which then triggers pupillary events.
source: Since MEG activity originates mostly in the cortex, the peak at –400 ms lag (100 ms earlier than the peak in monkey LC) could point to an influence of cortical resting state fluctuations on LC activity which then triggers pupillary events.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the relationship between cortical activity, LC activity, and pupil events.

claim: Pupil dilation and constriction events are controlled by sympathetic and parasympathetic pathways, respectively.
source: This result is surprising considering that pupil dilation and constriction events are controlled by sympathetic and parasympathetic pathways, respectively, activation of which is considered to have distinct effects on behavior ('fight or flight' vs. 'rest and digest').
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about autonomic nervous system control of pupil size.

claim: The sympathetic and parasympathetic pathways are indirectly affected by the shared neuromodulatory central arousal systems.
source: On the other hand, the sympathetic and parasympathetic pathways are also indirectly affected by the shared neuromodulatory central arousal systems (Lowenstein et al., 1963), and it is possible that in our task the pupillary dilation and constriction events merely reflect the adjustment of this central arousal state, not reaching the threshold of unique sympathetic or parasympathetic effects on behavior.
evidence: This claim is based on citation to Lowenstein et al., 1963 and speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Orientation tuning in V1 is better when a stimulus is presented during pupillary dilation as compared to constriction in mice.
source: A previous study in the mouse reported that orientation tuning in V1 is better when a stimulus is presented during pupillary dilation as compared to constriction (Reimer et al., 2014); however, it remains unknown if such improved tuning affects behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Reimer et al., 2014.

claim: The spectral power of cortical activity follows a 1/f function, the exponent of which links the power across frequencies.
source: Such a cross-frequency effect is consistent with intracranial EEG studies reporting that the spectral power of cortical activity follows a 1/f function, the exponent of which links the power across frequencies (He et al., 2010; Podvalny et al., 2015; Freeman and Zhai, 2009; He, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to intracranial EEG studies.
